fr:title.text: Poseidon, and Why Ethereum Walked Away

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Poseidon, and Why Ethereum Walked Away

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Poseidon (Grassi, Khovratovich, Rechberger, Roy, and Schofnegger, 2019) is a sponge over a prime field rather than over bits. Its permutation follows the HADES strategy: a few full rounds, where an S-box — typically x \mapsto x^5 — is applied to every element, and many partial rounds applying it to one, with an MDS matrix mixing the state between them. Poseidon2 later reworked the linear layer for speed. Because the whole function is field arithmetic, its cost inside a prime-field circuit is counted in multiplications, and it beat SHA-256 there by orders of magnitude.

The objection was always that the same algebraic structure that makes it cheap to arithmetise is what algebraic cryptanalysis attacks, and that parameters are generated per field and per state width rather than fixed once and studied for decades. The Ethereum Foundation took this seriously enough to fund the Poseidon Cryptanalysis Initiative, with bounties up to $1 million scheduled to run through December 2026.

It was paused on 1 August 2026, and on 13 August Justin Drake announced that the Foundation is abandoning Poseidon for L1 in favour of SHA or BLAKE, calling it "an epic 8-year, 8-figure rabbit hole in post-quantum cryptography" reaching "its dream conclusion." His diagnosis is the memorable part: "In hindsight the key was not SNARK-friendly hashes, but hash-friendly SNARKs."

What changed is the proving side. Binius moved the arithmetic into towers of binary fields, where a Boolean computation costs what it should instead of paying to embed single bits into a large prime field. Flock (eprint 2026/1329) took that further for the specific shape of the problem — large batches of the same Boolean circuit — and reports 82k BLAKE3 compressions, 42k SHA-256 compressions, and 30k Keccak permutations per second on one core of an M4 Max, more than 660k BLAKE3 compressions per second on ten, over 9 times faster than Binius64 on SHA-256 and more than 500 times faster than the fastest elliptic-curve SNARK it measured against. Drake's figure for the resulting designs is roughly one million conventional hash calls per second on a laptop, at about 100 times the cost of native execution.

Poseidon was not broken, and nothing here says it will be. An engineering decision was reversed because a different part of the stack improved, which is worth separating clearly from a cryptanalytic result — the security argument never changed, only what it had to buy. The stated roadmap puts a production-grade leanVM in 2027 and consensus, data, and execution layer deployment in 2028.
Sources: Drake's announcement, Flock and its implementation, the Poseidon Cryptanalysis Initiative.

fr:title.text: Hash Functions in Bitcoin and Ethereum

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Hash Functions in Bitcoin and Ethereum

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Both major chains rest on a handful of hash functions, and which one is never only a cryptographic question. Bitcoin runs SHA-256 for proof of work, transaction identifiers, and its Merkle trees, with RIPEMD-160 alongside it for addresses. Ethereum runs Keccak for addresses, storage slots, and the state trie, and SHA-256 on the consensus layer — two families inside one protocol.

What has been in flux is a third kind of hash. For most of a decade the argument was that a proof system wants a function designed for it: an arithmetisation-friendly hash like Poseidon, whose round function is cheap counted in field multiplications rather than bit operations. On 13 August 2026 the Ethereum Foundation abandoned that direction for L1. Justin Drake's announcement is the primary source for all of this, and his one-line summary is the clearest statement of the reversal — "the key was not SNARK-friendly hashes, but hash-friendly SNARKs."

The reason is not that Poseidon broke. Proof systems over binary fields closed the gap from the other side, so a conventional hash is now cheap enough to prove that its decades of public cryptanalysis are the deciding factor. SHA-2 and the BLAKE family are the candidates, and which BLAKE — 2s or 3 — is not settled in anything published so far.

SHA-256, published by NIST in 2001, is a Merkle–Damgård construction over a 64-round compression function on 32-bit words, absorbing 64 bytes per call. It is the most analysed hash in deployment, and Bitcoin has used nothing else for its core since 2009.

Bitcoin applies it twice — \mathrm {SHA256}(\mathrm {SHA256}(x)), usually written SHA-256d — for block headers and so for proof of work, for transaction identifiers, and for the Merkle tree committing a block's transactions. The usual rationale for the second application is length extension: a Merkle–Damgård hash leaks enough internal state that an attacker who knows H(m) can compute H(m \| p) for some padding p without knowing m, and hashing the digest again removes the property.

Addresses use a second family as well. The legacy scheme hashes a public key with \mathrm {RIPEMD160}(\mathrm {SHA256}(x)), which shortens the digest to 20 bytes and means a break of either function alone does not immediately yield a preimage. Taproot's tagged hashes (BIP-340) are built from SHA-256 with a domain-separation prefix, so even the newest parts of Bitcoin stay inside the same primitive.

The conservatism is the design. Twenty-five years of public cryptanalysis with no practical attack on the full function is a stronger argument than any efficiency claim, and it is the argument the 2026 Ethereum decision came back around to.

Ethereum's workhorse is keccak256, and it is not SHA-3. Keccak won the NIST competition in 2012, NIST changed the padding rule before standardising it as FIPS 202 in 2015, and Ethereum had already shipped the original. The two differ in padding and produce different digests for the same input, which is a reliable source of confusion for anyone reimplementing an Ethereum client.

It is used almost everywhere state is named. An address is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak digest of a public key; a mapping's storage slot is the digest of the key concatenated with the slot number; Merkle–Patricia trie nodes are addressed by the digest of their RLP encoding; function selectors and event topics are digest prefixes; and the KECCAK256 opcode exposes it to contracts directly.

The consensus layer chose differently. SSZ's hash_tree_root is SHA-256, so a full node computes both families — Keccak for execution state and SHA-256 for beacon state. The EVM also exposes SHA-256 and RIPEMD-160 as precompiles at 0x02 and 0x03, and BLAKE2b's compression function at 0x09 (EIP-152, Istanbul, December 2019, priced at one gas per round).

For a prover this split matters, because the execution state is the Keccak half. Keccak is the most expensive of the three to prove — Flock reports 30k Keccak permutations per second per core against 42k SHA-256 compressions — though the gap per byte is narrower than the raw rates suggest, since one Keccak-256 permutation absorbs 136 bytes where a SHA-256 compression takes 64.

BLAKE was a SHA-3 finalist that lost to Keccak and then outlived the defeat. BLAKE2 (2013) cut the round count — 12 rounds where BLAKE had 16, or 10 where it had 14 — and dropped the HAIFA counter and constant additions for speed. BLAKE3 (2020) went further, to seven rounds, and replaced the serial mode with a tree.

The 2s and 2b split is a word-size split, and it is the detail that matters for the current Ethereum discussion.
BLAKE2b — 64-bit words, 1024-bit state, 128-byte blocks, 12 rounds, digests of any length from 1 to 64 bytes. Tuned for 64-bit CPUs.
BLAKE2s — 32-bit words, 512-bit state, 64-byte blocks, 10 rounds, digests of 1 to 32 bytes. Intended for 8- to 32-bit platforms, so it is the variant that suits constrained environments. Collision resistance follows the digest: up to 256 bits for 2b, up to 128 for 2s.

Both carry machinery that SHA-2 lacks. Keying is built into the compression function, so BLAKE2 is a MAC without needing HMAC around it, and the parameter block also takes a salt and a personalisation string, which gives domain separation for free rather than by convention. The family also includes parallel variants (BLAKE2sp, BLAKE2bp) and an extendable-output construction, BLAKE2X. In deployment, WireGuard uses BLAKE2s — 32-byte digests for hashing, keyed with 16-byte output as a MAC — and Zcash uses BLAKE2b for Equihash and for key derivation.

BLAKE3 keeps BLAKE2s's 32-bit words and 64-byte block and cuts to seven rounds, then splits the input into 1 KiB chunks arranged in a binary tree. That is what makes it parallel over any number of cores, incremental, and usable as an extendable-output function from a single algorithm rather than a family of them. The seven-round decision is the contested one: the designers argue the cryptanalysis supports it, and it is also the reason BLAKE3 has the least margin of anything in this note.

Which BLAKE Ethereum is actually considering is not yet public. Drake's announcement says "SHA or BLAKE"; some coverage reports the candidates as SHA-2 or BLAKE2s, other coverage says BLAKE3, and published benchmark comparisons put SHA-256, Keccak, BLAKE3 and leanXMSS side by side. The one thing that is clear is that the variant already in the EVM is not the one in question: EIP-152 exposes BLAKE2b's compression function at 0x09, added for Zcash interoperability, and BLAKE2b is the 64-bit variant that neither candidate set names.

My guess at the reasoning, which is inference and not something I have seen argued: for hash-based signatures the inputs are short and fixed-size, a 32-byte block at a time, so BLAKE3's chunking and tree mode buy nothing and only add constraints, while BLAKE2s gives the same 32-bit word size with three more rounds of margin and a decade of analysis. If the deciding workload is signature verification rather than hashing long messages, the tree is dead weight.
Sources: BLAKE2, the BLAKE3 specification draft, EIP-152.

Prime fields, extension fields, and why the prover wants a small base field while soundness wants a large challenge space.

Where extension-field arithmetic is unavoidable — challenges, DEEP queries, batching — and how much of the trace can stay in the base field.
Packing and vectorisation: how field choice interacts with the machine.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Soundness Regimes and the Proximity-Gap Conjectures

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The same protocol has different soundness depending on how far from the code you are willing to reason, and the parameters used in production sit in the regime where the analysis is conjectural. This page is the reason list decoding is in this corpus at all.

Questions this page should answer:
Unique decoding, the Johnson bound, and capacity: the guarantee each yields and the parameters each licenses.
What must be conjectured to reach capacity, and the precise statement of each conjecture.
Threshold halving, and what it establishes above the Johnson bound.
The accounting from soundness error to bits of security, including grinding.
Which deployed systems set parameters in which regime — and whether the choice is documented anywhere citable.
Sources: SoK: Hash-Based Polynomial Commitments, On Reed–Solomon Proximity Gaps Conjectures, FRI Soundness Above the Johnson Bound.
